lesson_title: Two WhatsApp Groups and the Double-Counted Friends
hook_text: 75 in one group. 60 in the other. That's NOT 135 people — and the reason is a rule that runs half of probability.
clip_script: You're in two WhatsApp groups. Cricket group: 75 members. Rugby group: 60. So that's 135 people, right? Wrong — and the reason is one of the most-tested rules in high school maths. Twenty-five people are in BOTH groups. Their names sit on the cricket list AND the rugby list — so when you added the lists, you counted every one of them twice. The honest headcount: 75 plus 60, MINUS the 25 double-counted friends. One hundred and ten real people. That subtraction has a name — the addition rule: probability of A or B equals probability of A, plus probability of B, minus probability of A and B. The minus exists for exactly one reason: to cancel the double-count. Draw it as two overlapping circles: fill the overlap first — 25 — then subtract outwards: 50 cricket-only, 35 rugby-only, and 40 people outside both. Four regions, everyone in exactly one. When can you skip the minus? Only when the groups share NOBODY — mutually exclusive — because then the overlap is zero and the minus deletes itself. Never count anyone twice. That one sentence is worth more marks than you'd believe.
visual_style: Two glowing chat-group icons overlap like a Venn diagram; duplicated avatar faces flash red in the overlap, a giant minus sign sweeps them away, and the four regions light up with their counts.
pacing: Fast setup, record-scratch on 'Wrong', rhythmic fill-the-regions sequence, clean rule reveal at the end.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never double-count again.
